title: Modals of obligation and advice
objectives: Distinguish obligation, prohibition and lack of obligation.
Form questions and negatives with have to.

explanation.heading: Meaning and use
paragraphs: We use must and have to to express obligation or necessity. ‘You must wear a seat belt’ states a strong requirement. ‘I have to leave at six because my shift starts at seven’ describes something necessary in my situation. The difference between must and have to is not fixed: both can express rules or obligations, and the choice depends on context and the speaker's view.

Use should for advice or a recommendation: ‘You should take a break’. It is generally less forceful than must. You can advise against something with shouldn't: ‘You shouldn't work all night’. Advice is not necessarily a rule.

explanation.heading: Form
paragraphs: Must and should are modal verbs. They do not change after he or she, and they are followed by the base form: ‘She must leave’ and ‘He should rest’. Their negatives are must not or mustn't, and should not or shouldn't. Questions put the modal before the subject: ‘Should I call?’ and ‘Must we leave now?’

Have to behaves differently. Use have to with I, you, we and they, and has to with he, she, it and singular nouns: ‘She has to work’. For a present question or negative, use do or does: ‘Does she have to work?’ and ‘She doesn't have to work’. In the past, had to can express necessity: ‘We had to leave early yesterday’.

explanation.heading: Examples in context
paragraphs: The negative meanings differ. Mustn't means something is prohibited: ‘You mustn't park here’ means parking is not allowed. Don't have to means there is no obligation: ‘You don't have to bring food’ means food is optional; bringing it is not prohibited. Read signs and instructions carefully, because these meanings are very different.

Look at the examples below. ‘You should drink some water’ is advice. ‘You have to show a ticket’ describes a requirement. ‘You don't have to print the ticket’ removes an obligation. A person could still choose to print it unless another rule says otherwise.

explanation.heading: Contrasts and common mistakes
paragraphs: Do not add to after must or should: ‘must go’ and ‘should go’, not ‘must to go’ or ‘should to go’. Do not add -s to the main verb after these modals: ‘He must work’. In contrast, have to changes to has to with he and she.

Mustn't and don't have to are not interchangeable. Also, advice and rules can be expressed in other ways: ‘You need to leave’ may describe necessity, while ‘It would be a good idea to leave’ suggests advice. Tone, context and the source of a rule help the listener understand how strong an instruction is.

examples.sentence: Passengers must wear a seat belt.
I have to start work at seven.
She has to show her ticket.
examples.note: A singular subject takes has to.

examples.sentence: You don't have to print the ticket.

examples.note: Should comes before the subject in the question.

examples.sentence: We had to leave early yesterday.
examples.note: Had to expresses a past necessity.

common_errors.reason: Use the base verb without to after must.

common_errors.incorrect: You mustn’t bring food. It is optional.
common_errors.correct: You don’t have to bring food. It is optional.
common_errors.reason: Don’t have to expresses no obligation; mustn’t prohibits it.

summary: Use must or have to for obligation and should for advice.
Mustn’t expresses prohibition; don’t have to expresses no obligation.
Use the base verb after must and should, but use have to or has to as appropriate.

exercises.prompt: The sign says parking is prohibited. You ___ park here.

option_feedback.a: “don’t have to” does not fit here. Mustn’t expresses prohibition.
option_feedback.b: “should” does not fit here. Mustn’t expresses prohibition.
option_feedback.d: “can” does not fit here. Mustn’t expresses prohibition.

exercises.prompt: Printing is optional. You ___ print the ticket.
exercises.explanation: Don’t have to means there is no obligation.

option_feedback.a: “don’t have to” fits here. Don’t have to means there is no obligation.
option_feedback.b: “mustn’t” does not fit here. Don’t have to means there is no obligation.
option_feedback.c: “must” does not fit here. Don’t have to means there is no obligation.
option_feedback.d: “have to” does not fit here. Don’t have to means there is no obligation.

exercises.prompt: I advise you to rest. You ___ take a break.

option_feedback.a: “mustn’t” does not fit here. Should expresses advice.
option_feedback.b: “have not to” does not fit here. Should expresses advice.
option_feedback.c: “should to” does not fit here. Should expresses advice.

exercises.prompt: Company rules require Mia to wear a badge. She ___ wear one.
exercises.explanation: Has to expresses the requirement with she.

option_feedback.a: “have to” does not fit here. Has to expresses the requirement with she.
option_feedback.b: “has to” fits here. Has to expresses the requirement with she.
option_feedback.c: “should to” does not fit here. Has to expresses the requirement with she.
option_feedback.d: “musts” does not fit here. Has to expresses the requirement with she.

exercises.prompt: ___ she have to work on Sunday?
exercises.explanation: Does introduces the question with she; use have to.

option_feedback.a: “Does” fits here. Does introduces the question with she; use have to.
option_feedback.b: “Must to” does not fit here. Does introduces the question with she; use have to.
option_feedback.c: “Do” does not fit here. Does introduces the question with she; use have to.
option_feedback.d: “Is” does not fit here. Does introduces the question with she; use have to.

exercises.prompt: We ___ leave early yesterday because the office closed.

option_feedback.a: “must to” does not fit here. Had to expresses past necessity.
option_feedback.b: “has to” does not fit here. Had to expresses past necessity.
option_feedback.c: “had to” fits here. Had to expresses past necessity.
option_feedback.d: “shoulds” does not fit here. Had to expresses past necessity.

exercises.prompt: You ___ touch the wire. The sign says it is prohibited.

option_feedback.a: “don’t have to” does not fit here. Mustn’t expresses prohibition.
option_feedback.b: “should” does not fit here. Mustn’t expresses prohibition.
option_feedback.c: “may” does not fit here. Mustn’t expresses prohibition.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence gives advice?
exercises.explanation: Should is followed by the base verb rest.

option_feedback.a: “You shoulds rest.” does not fit here. Should is followed by the base verb rest.
option_feedback.b: “You should rest.” fits here. Should is followed by the base verb rest.
option_feedback.c: “You should to rest.” does not fit here. Should is followed by the base verb rest.
option_feedback.d: “You should rests.” does not fit here. Should is followed by the base verb rest.

Choose mustn’t or don’t have to: Parking is prohibited; you ___ park here.

exercises.explanation: Don’t have to expresses no obligation.

Complete with have or has: She ___ to leave now.
Complete with do or does: ___ he have to work tomorrow?
